references.text: The preceding questioning of John about his identity—whether he was the Christ, Elijah, or the Prophet—forms the background for the question in verse 25. They had already received his answers, and now they logically ask further: Why then do you baptize? See [ref:Joh 1:19-22|John 1:19-22].

John explains that his water baptism was given to him by God who sent him, and that it pointed toward the one who would baptize with the Holy Spirit. This indirectly answers the question about his authority to baptize; see [ref:Joh 1:33|John 1:33].

Jesus himself asked a similar question about John's baptism—where it came from, from heaven or from men—which shows that the issue of John's authority to baptize was a recurring theme; see [ref:Matt 21:25|Matthew 21:25].

Matthew describes John's baptismal ministry where people were baptized in the Jordan and confessed their sins, thus providing context for the baptism that the Pharisees questioned; see [ref:Matt 3:5-6|Matthew 3:5-6].

Moses' promise that the Lord will raise up a prophet like himself is the background for the term "the Prophet" (ὁ προφήτης) mentioned in the verse. The Pharisees expected this prophet to have special authority, perhaps even to institute rituals such as baptism; see [ref:5 Mos 18:15-18|Deuteronomy 18:15-18].

The expectation of Elijah's coming before the Lord's great day is the background for the question about whether John was Elijah, and thus whether he had authority to baptize; see [ref:Mal 4:5|Malachi 4:5].

Paul meets disciples in Ephesus who knew only of John's baptism, showing that John's baptism was widespread and raised questions about its authority and relationship to the Messiah; see [ref:Apg 19:1-4|Acts 19:1-4].

God's promise to sprinkle clean water over the people to cleanse them is part of the prophetic background for an eschatological cleansing that the Pharisees may have associated with the work of the Messiah or the coming Prophet; see [ref:Esek 36:25|Ezekiel 36:25].
